courses.title: Ch 4 · Political Parties
courses.summary: What political parties are and do, why democracies need them, kinds of party systems, recognition of national and state parties by the Election Commission, the challenges parties face and how they can be reformed.
outcomes: Learners can define a political party and list its functions
Learners can compare one-party, two-party and multi-party systems
Learners can state the criteria for national and state party recognition
Learners can analyse challenges to parties and suggest reforms

lessons.title: Why do we need political parties?

scenes.text: Imagine every MP elected as an independent. Who would form the government?
Each would promise something different – no one could be held responsible.

steps.title: Meaning and components
steps.body: A **political party** is a group of people who come together to contest elections and hold power in the government. They agree on some policies and programmes for society with a view to promote the collective good. Parties reflect fundamental political divisions in society; a party is known by which part it stands for, which policies it supports and whose interests it upholds – **partisanship**. A party has three components: the **leaders**, the **active members** and the **followers**.

steps.title: Functions and necessity
steps.body:
**Functions:**
1. **Contest elections** – candidates are put up by parties (in India chosen by top leaders; in the USA, members and supporters choose).
2. Put forward different **policies and programmes**; voters choose among them.
3. Play a decisive role in **making laws** – MPs follow party leadership.
4. **Form and run governments** – recruit and train leaders.
5. Those that lose play the role of **opposition** – voice different views and criticise the government.
6. **Shape public opinion** – raise and highlight issues; launch movements.
7. Provide people **access to government machinery and welfare schemes** – local party leaders are easy to approach.

**Necessity:** without parties every candidate would be independent; no one could make promises about major policy changes; the government's utility would be uncertain and no one would be accountable. Parties emerged with representative democracy, which needs a way to gather different views and to support or restrain the government.

steps.title: Solved example: List four functions of political parties (4 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Contest elections and put up candidates.

**Step 2:** Put forward policies and programmes.

**Step 3:** Make laws and form/run governments.

**Step 4:** Act as opposition and shape public opinion (also: give access to welfare schemes).

steps.title: Solved example: Why is a democracy without parties impractical? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Every candidate would be independent; no common policy direction.

**Step 2:** No one could be held responsible for how the country is run.

**Step 3:** Large societies need representative government – parties organise views and leadership for it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the three components: **leaders, active members, followers**.
- Saying only the ruling party matters – the opposition is a key function too.

activity.prompt: Check if a group is a political party – does it…
items: Have a set of policies and programmes?
Have leaders, active members and followers?
Represent a section of society's view (partisanship)?

quiz.q: Partisanship means
options: being inclined to a particular side
quiz.why: Partisanship means being inclined to a particular side, which is a mark of political parties.

quiz.q: The three components of a party are
quiz.why: A political party has three components: leaders, active members and followers.

quiz.q: In the USA, party candidates are chosen by
quiz.why: In the USA party candidates are chosen by members and supporters in primary elections.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a function of parties?
quiz.why: Delivering court judgements is the work of the judiciary, not of political parties.

quiz.q: Parties emerged along with
quiz.why: Political parties emerged along with the rise of representative democracies.

scenes.text: In China, only the Communist Party is allowed to rule.
In India, dozens of parties compete and often govern in alliances.

steps.title: Kinds of party systems
steps.body:
- **One-party system:** only one party is allowed to control and run the government – e.g. **China** (Communist Party). It is not a good option for democracy because there is no free competition.
- **Two-party system:** power usually changes between two main parties; others exist but only two have a serious chance of winning a majority – e.g. **USA, UK**.
- **Multi-party system:** several parties compete for power, and more than two have a reasonable chance of coming to power either on their own or in alliance – e.g. **India**. When several parties form an **alliance or front** to contest elections and win power, the government is a **coalition** – e.g. **NDA, UPA, Left Front**. Multi-party systems may look messy and lead to instability, but they allow a variety of interests and opinions to enjoy representation.

The party system is not chosen by a country; it evolves over a long time depending on society, its social and regional divisions, its history and its electoral system.

steps.title: Solved example: Why does India have a multi-party system? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Social and geographical diversity – many communities, languages and regions.

**Step 2:** Such diversity cannot easily be absorbed by two or three parties.

**Step 3:** The system evolved over time; it allows varied interests to be represented, often via coalitions.

steps.title: Solved example: Compare two-party and multi-party systems (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Two-party:** two main parties alternate in power (USA, UK); clear choice, stable majorities.

**Step 2 – Multi-party:** several parties with real chances; coalitions common (India).

**Step 3 – Trade-off:** multi-party gives wider representation but may be less stable.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying a country “chooses” its party system – it **evolves** over time.
- Calling China a two-party system – it is a **one-party** system.

activity.prompt: Match the country to its party system

quiz.q: A one-party system exists in
quiz.why: China has a one-party system, where only one party is allowed to control the government.

quiz.q: A coalition government is formed by
quiz.why: A coalition government is formed by an alliance of parties.

quiz.q: NDA and UPA are examples of
quiz.why: The NDA and UPA are alliances of parties, formed to contest elections or run governments together.

quiz.q: A merit of multi-party systems is
quiz.why: A merit of a multi-party system is that it represents a variety of interests and opinions.

quiz.q: Party systems
options: are chosen by law in a day
quiz.why: Party systems evolve over a long time, depending on the history, society and election system.

scenes.text: At the polling booth, Arjun sees symbols on the EVM next to each candidate.
Only recognised parties get a unique symbol reserved across a state or the country.

steps.title: Recognition by the Election Commission
steps.body:
Every party must **register** with the **Election Commission (EC)**. Larger, established parties are given **recognition** – a unique symbol that only their official candidates can use, and other facilities.

- **State party:** a party that secures at least **6% of the total votes** in an election to the Legislative Assembly of a State and wins **at least two seats**.
- **National party:** a party that secures at least **6% of the total votes in Lok Sabha elections or Assembly elections in four States** and wins **at least four seats in the Lok Sabha**.

Recognition changes after elections. As of the Election Commission's April 2023 update, the recognised national parties were **Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP), Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), Communist Party of India (Marxist) – CPI(M), Indian National Congress (INC) and National People's Party (NPP)**. Always check the EC's latest list.

State parties (often called regional parties) have grown in importance; since 1996 nearly every state party has had a chance to be part of one or another national coalition government, strengthening federalism and democracy.

steps.title: Some national parties (brief profiles)
steps.body:
- **INC (1885):** one of the oldest parties; dominated Indian politics for decades after Independence; centrist ideology; led the UPA (2004–2014).
- **BJP (1980):** founded reviving the Bharatiya Jana Sangh (1951, Syama Prasad Mukherjee); cultural nationalism; leads the NDA; formed governments from 2014.
- **BSP (1984):** formed under **Kanshi Ram**; seeks to represent and secure power for the bahujan samaj (Dalits, Adivasis, OBCs, religious minorities); inspired by Sahu Maharaj, Phule, Periyar, Ambedkar.
- **CPI(M) (1964):** believes in Marxism–Leninism; supports socialism, secularism and democracy; strong in West Bengal, Kerala, Tripura in the past.
- **NPP (2013):** first party from the north-east to attain national party status (2019).
- **AAP (2012):** recognised as a national party in 2023.

steps.title: Solved example: A party gets 7% votes and 3 seats in one state assembly election. Is it a state party? (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Criteria:** at least 6% votes AND at least 2 seats in that state's assembly election.

**Step 2 – Check:** 7% ≥ 6% and 3 ≥ 2 → **yes, it qualifies** as a state party.

steps.title: Solved example: A party wins 6% votes in Lok Sabha elections but only 3 Lok Sabha seats. Does it meet that national-party criterion? (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Criterion (as given in NCERT):** 6% votes in Lok Sabha or Assembly elections in four states AND at least 4 Lok Sabha seats.

**Step 2 – Check:** only 3 seats → **does not meet** this criterion.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the **seats** condition – votes alone are not enough.
- Listing old national parties from memory without checking the year – recognition **changes after elections**.

activity.prompt: A party needs at least 6% of 5,00,000 votes cast in a state assembly election to meet the vote condition for state recognition. Minimum votes needed?

quiz.q: Recognition of parties is given by
quiz.why: The Election Commission recognises parties as state or national parties.

quiz.q: A state party needs at least what share of votes in an assembly election?
quiz.why: A state party must win at least 6% of the votes in an assembly election and at least 2 seats.

quiz.q: A national party must win at least how many Lok Sabha seats (with the vote criterion)?
quiz.why: A national party must win at least 4 Lok Sabha seats along with the vote criterion.

quiz.q: BSP was formed under the leadership of
quiz.why: Kanshi Ram led the formation of the BSP in 1984.

quiz.q: Which was the first party from the north-east to get national status?
quiz.why: The National People's Party became the first party from the north-east to get national status.

scenes.text: A party gives a ticket to a leader's son over a long-serving worker.
Workers protest about lack of internal democracy.

steps.title: Four challenges
steps.body:
1. **Lack of internal democracy:** power concentrated in one or a few leaders; no regular organisational meetings or internal elections; ordinary members don't get information; dissenters find it difficult to continue.
2. **Dynastic succession:** top positions controlled by members of one family; unfair to other members and bad for democracy.
3. **Growing role of money and muscle power:** parties nominate candidates who can raise money; rich people and companies influence policies; sometimes parties support criminals who can win elections.
4. **Lack of meaningful choice:** ideological differences among parties have reduced in many parts of the world; voters can't find very different options; even leaders keep shifting between parties.

steps.title: Reforms
steps.body:
**Steps taken:**
- **Anti-defection law** – the Constitution was amended so that if an MLA or MP changes parties, he or she loses the seat. (Side effect: it strengthened party leaders, as members must accept whatever leaders decide.)
- The **Supreme Court** ordered that every candidate file an **affidavit** giving details of property and criminal cases pending – the information is made public (but there is no system to check its truth).
- The **Election Commission** made it necessary for parties to hold organisational elections and file **income tax returns**.

**Suggestions:** a law to regulate internal affairs of parties (register members, follow own constitution, independent authority, open elections to highest posts); a minimum number of tickets (about **one-third**) to women candidates and quotas within party decision-making bodies; **state funding of elections** (government gives parties money – in kind such as petrol, paper, telephone – or cash based on votes). Two other ways: **pressure from people** (petitions, publicity, agitations; media, movements) and **people joining parties** to improve them.

steps.title: Solved example: Suggest three reforms for political parties (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Law to regulate internal affairs – member registers, internal elections, independent authority.

**Step 2:** Reserve about one-third of tickets for women; quotas in party bodies.

**Step 3:** State funding of elections to reduce money power.

steps.title: Solved example: What is the anti-defection law and what is its side effect? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Meaning:** an MP/MLA who changes party after election loses the seat.

**Step 2 – Aim:** stop defections driven by money or office.

**Step 3 – Side effect:** it increased the power of party leaders – members must follow the leadership even when they disagree.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the Election Commission introduced affidavits – it was a **Supreme Court** order.
- Claiming the anti-defection law has no drawback – it has made leaders more powerful.

activity.prompt: Challenge or reform?

items.text: Affidavit on assets and criminal cases

quiz.why: The anti-defection law disqualifies a legislator who changes party after being elected.

quiz.why: The Supreme Court ordered candidates to file affidavits on their assets and criminal cases.

top posts are controlled by one family
quiz.why: Dynastic succession is a challenge because top posts are held by members of one family, which is unfair to others.

quiz.q: State funding of elections aims to
quiz.why: State funding of elections aims to reduce parties' dependence on big donors, and so reduces the role of money.

quiz.q: The EC requires parties to
options: hold organisational elections and file IT returns
quiz.why: The Election Commission requires parties to hold organisational elections and file income tax returns, for transparency.

questions.why: A political party is a group of people who come together to contest elections and hold power.

questions.q: India has a
questions.why: India has a multi-party system, as many parties compete and have a chance of power.

questions.why: The opposition criticises the government and voices different views, and also mobilises public opinion.

questions.q: The USA and UK are examples of
questions.why: The USA and the UK have two main parties competing for power, so they are two-party systems.

questions.q: Which challenge refers to reduced ideological differences among parties?

questions.q: Assertion: Multi-party systems often lead to coalitions. Reason: More than two parties have a reasonable chance of power.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. When more than two parties have a reasonable chance of power, no single party may win a majority, so coalitions form.

questions.q: Assertion: The anti-defection law ended all problems of parties. Reason: It made party leaders more powerful.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: The anti-defection law did not end all problems of parties, so A is false. It did make party leaders more powerful, so R is true.

questions.q: Case: A party has no internal elections for 20 years and expels members who disagree. The challenge is
questions.why: Not holding internal elections for years and expelling dissenters shows lack of internal democracy.

questions.q: Which statement about recognition is correct?
options: Recognised parties get a reserved symbol
questions.why: A recognised party gets a reserved symbol and other benefits from the Election Commission.

questions.q: Which was founded in 1984 to represent the bahujan samaj?
questions.why: The BSP was founded in 1984 to represent the bahujan samaj.

questions.q: Which reform targets money power directly?
questions.why: State funding of elections directly addresses money power by reducing dependence on rich donors.

questions.why: A state party needs both 6% of the votes and 2 seats. With only 1 seat, it does not qualify.

questions.q: Out of 10,00,000 votes in a state, a party gets 55,000 and 2 seats. Does it meet the 6% + 2 seats rule?
options: No – it has only 5.5% of votes

questions.q: Why might parties nominate candidates with criminal records, according to NCERT?

courses.title: Ch 5 · Outcomes of Democracy
courses.summary: How to assess democracy: accountable, responsive and legitimate government; economic growth and development; reduction of inequality and poverty; accommodation of social diversity; and the dignity and freedom of citizens.
outcomes: Learners can explain why democracy produces accountable, responsive and legitimate government
Learners can evaluate democracy's record on growth, inequality and poverty
Learners can explain how democracy accommodates social diversity
Learners can describe how democracy promotes dignity and freedom of citizens

scenes.text: Kavita files an RTI application asking why her village road has not been built.
Within weeks she gets the file details – the money was never released.

steps.title: How to assess democracy
steps.body:
Democracy is preferred over other forms because it promotes **equality among citizens**, enhances the **dignity of the individual**, improves the **quality of decision-making**, provides a method to **resolve conflicts** and allows room to **correct mistakes**. We should expect democracy to produce certain outcomes, but not everything – it creates conditions for achieving goals; citizens must use them.

**Accountable government:** citizens have the right and means to examine the process of decision-making – **transparency**. Decisions are taken according to norms and procedures. Democratic governments may be slower (delays due to deliberation and negotiation) but decisions are more acceptable and effective.

**Responsive government:** attentive to people's needs and demands; regular, free and fair elections; open public debate on major policies and legislation; citizens' right to information about the government. Records are mixed – democracies do not always meet people's expectations or address majority needs.

**Legitimate government:** democracy's outcome that it is the people's own government. Though slow, less efficient and not always responsive or clean, democracy enjoys support all over the world – people want to be ruled by representatives elected by them.

steps.title: Solved example: Why are democratic decisions slower but better? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Slower:** deliberation and negotiation among many people and procedures take time.

**Step 2 – Better:** decisions follow norms and are transparent; affected people are consulted.

**Step 3 – Result:** they are more acceptable and more effective in implementation.

steps.title: Solved example: Give two mechanisms that make governments accountable (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Regular free and fair elections – voters can remove the government.

**Step 2:** Right to information and open public debate – citizens can examine decisions.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying democracy guarantees all problems are solved – it creates **conditions**; citizens must use them.
- Equating efficiency with legitimacy – a non-democratic regime may be quick but is not legitimate.

activity.prompt: Which outcome does it show?

items.text: Citizens can see how decisions are made (transparency)
People accept the government as their own

quiz.q: Transparency means
quiz.why: Transparency means citizens can examine the process of decision-making.

quiz.q: Democratic decisions may be slow because of
quiz.why: Democratic decisions can be slow because of consultation, deliberation and negotiation.

quiz.q: A legitimate government is
quiz.why: A legitimate government is the people's own government, elected and accepted by them.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a reason democracy is preferred?
quiz.why: Democracy does not promise to never make mistakes. It lets mistakes be corrected, promotes equality and enhances dignity.

quiz.q: Responsive government means
quiz.why: A responsive government is attentive to the needs and demands of the people.

scenes.text: A dictatorship's economy grows fast for a few years; a democracy grows steadily.
But in both, the poorest families still struggle.

steps.title: Growth and development
steps.body: If democracies are expected to produce good governments, are they also expected to produce development? Evidence shows that over a long period (NCERT cites 1950–2000) **dictatorships have slightly higher rates of economic growth**. But that alone is not reason to reject democracy: economic development depends on many factors – a country's population size, global situation, cooperation from other countries, economic priorities. The difference between growth rates of the two is negligible. Democracy is preferable because it has several other positive outcomes.

steps.title: Inequality and poverty
steps.body:
- Democracies are based on **political equality** – every citizen has equal weight in electing representatives. But **economic inequalities** have grown: a small number of ultra-rich enjoy a highly disproportionate share of wealth and incomes, and their share is increasing; those at the bottom have very little to depend on.
- Democracies have not been very successful in reducing economic inequalities. In actual life, the poor constitute a large proportion of voters and no party wants to lose their votes, yet democratically elected governments do not appear as keen to address poverty as expected.
- In some countries like **Bangladesh**, more than half the population lived in poverty (NCERT data); people in several poor countries depend on rich countries even for food supplies.

steps.title: Solved example: “Dictatorships grow faster, so they are better.” Evaluate (4 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Evidence:** dictatorships have only slightly higher growth – the difference is negligible.

**Step 2 – Other factors:** growth depends on population, global situation, cooperation and priorities.

**Step 3 – Other outcomes:** democracy gives dignity, freedom, accountability, legitimacy.

**Step 4 – Conclusion:** growth rates alone cannot justify rejecting democracy.

steps.title: Solved example: Why has democracy not reduced poverty much? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Political equality does not automatically bring economic equality.

**Step 2:** The ultra-rich hold a growing share of wealth and influence policy.

**Step 3:** Governments are not as keen to address poverty as expected, though the poor are a large share of voters.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing that democracies always have faster growth – evidence shows **slightly lower** growth on average, but a negligible difference.
- Confusing political equality (one vote) with economic equality.

statements.s: Dictatorships have slightly higher growth rates on average (NCERT evidence).
Democracy guarantees economic equality.
Growth depends on many factors besides the type of government.
The poor are a small share of voters.

quiz.q: Political equality means
quiz.why: Political equality means every vote has equal weight, as in one person, one vote.

quiz.q: Economic growth depends on
options: many factors like population and global situation
quiz.why: Economic growth depends on many factors, such as population size, global conditions and cooperation from other countries.

quiz.q: A small number of ultra-rich holding a large share of wealth shows
quiz.why: A tiny group of very rich people holding a large share of wealth is economic inequality.

quiz.q: The growth difference between democracies and dictatorships is
quiz.why: The difference in growth between democracies and dictatorships is small, so it is negligible.

quiz.q: Assertion: Democracy should not be rejected for slower growth. Reason: It has other positive outcomes like dignity and accountability.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
quiz.why: Both are true. Democracy should not be rejected for slower growth, because it has other positive outcomes like dignity and accountability.

lessons.title: Accommodation of diversity; dignity and freedom

scenes.text: At the polling booth, a Dalit grandmother and a rich businessman stand in the same queue.
Each vote has the same value.

steps.title: Accommodation of social diversity
steps.body:
Democracies usually develop a procedure to conduct their competition, which reduces the possibility of tensions becoming explosive or violent. No society can fully and permanently resolve conflicts among groups, but democracies are best at handling social differences, divisions and conflicts (e.g. Belgium).

Conditions: (1) democracy is not simply rule by majority opinion – the majority must work with the minority so governments represent the general view; (2) rule by majority does not mean rule by a majority community (religion, race, linguistic group); everyone should have a chance to be in the majority at some time. If someone is barred from being in the majority on the basis of birth, the rule ceases to be accommodative.

steps.title: Dignity and freedom of citizens
steps.body:
Democracy stands much superior to any other form in promoting **dignity and freedom of the individual**. Every individual wants respect from fellow beings.

- **Dignity of women:** most societies were male-dominated; long struggles have created some sensitivity that respect and equal treatment of women are necessary ingredients of a democratic society. It is now possible for women to wage a struggle against discrimination, legally and morally.
- **Caste inequalities:** democracy in India has strengthened the claims of disadvantaged and discriminated castes for equal status and opportunity. Instances of caste discrimination and atrocities persist, but these lack the moral and legal foundations.
- Democracy is a continuous process: as people get some benefits, they ask for more – complaints about democracy are a testimony to its success, showing people have become conscious and critical.

steps.title: Solved example: Two conditions for democracy to accommodate diversity (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** The majority must work with the minority – rule is not simply majority opinion.

**Step 2:** Majority must not be a fixed community by birth; everyone should get a chance to be in the majority.

steps.title: Solved example: “Complaints about democracy are a testimony to its success.” Explain (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Democracy makes people aware of their rights and expectations.

**Step 2:** As they get some benefits, they demand more – they become critical observers.

**Step 3:** People in non-democracies often cannot complain; complaints show a free, engaged citizenry.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking democracy means rule by a majority **community** – it means majority **opinion** that changes, with minority views respected.
- Saying caste discrimination has ended – it persists but has lost moral and legal backing.

a.text: In a town council, the majority community proposes that only its festivals get public funds.

choices.label: Support it – majority rules
choices.feedback: Rule by a fixed majority community is not accommodative.

choices.label: Propose fair funding for all communities' festivals
choices.feedback: This lets every group be respected.

b.text: The minority feels excluded and protests. What do you do?

choices.label: Invite all groups to agree on fair rules together
choices.feedback: Democracies resolve conflicts through procedures and negotiation.

c.text: The council adopts fair rules. Democracy accommodated diversity: the majority worked with the minority.

d.text: Tensions rise. Democracy is not rule by a majority community. Try the accommodative path.

quiz.q: Democracies handle social differences by
quiz.why: Democracies manage social differences by providing procedures for peaceful competition and negotiation.

quiz.q: Majority rule in a democracy should mean
quiz.why: Majority rule means following the majority opinion while respecting the minority, and the majority must change over time.

quiz.q: Democracy has strengthened claims of
quiz.why: Democracy has strengthened the claims of disadvantaged castes for equal status and opportunity.

quiz.q: Complaints about democracy show
options: its success – citizens are aware and critical
quiz.why: Complaints about democracy show that citizens are aware and critical, which is a sign of its success.

quiz.q: Which country's example shows successful accommodation (Ch 1)?
quiz.why: Belgium's power-sharing arrangement is the example of successful accommodation of diversity.

scenes.text: Topic: "Democracy is the best form of government". Raghav must argue both sides.
He prepares points on outcomes, with evidence.

steps.title: Framework for evaluation
steps.body:
Use the five outcomes as headings: (1) accountable, responsive, legitimate government; (2) economic growth and development; (3) reduction of inequality and poverty; (4) accommodation of social diversity; (5) dignity and freedom of citizens.

For each, give: **expectation → evidence → assessment**. Democracy scores well on legitimacy, accommodation, dignity and freedom; mixed on responsiveness; not much better than dictatorships on growth and inequality. Overall, democracy's strength lies in providing a process to correct mistakes and enabling citizens to demand more.

steps.title: Solved example: Case: A democratic government delays a dam to hold public hearings. Critics call it inefficient. Respond (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Accept the cost:** deliberation takes time.

**Step 2 – Benefit:** affected people are heard; decisions become transparent and acceptable.

**Step 3 – Conclusion:** slower but more effective and legitimate – an outcome of accountable government.

steps.title: Solved example: Case: In a democracy, ultra-rich groups gain while poverty persists. Which outcome is weak? (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Reduction of inequality and poverty.

**Step 2:** Political equality exists but economic inequality persists – democracy has not done well here.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Giving only praise – a good evaluation includes **limitations**.
- Forgetting to use the RTI/transparency example when discussing accountability.

Slightly lower than dictatorships, negligible difference
Women and Dalits claim equal status

quiz.why: Democracy scores best on legitimacy and the dignity of citizens. It does not promise fastest growth or an end to poverty.

quiz.q: The RTI example best supports

quiz.q: A strong evaluation should include
quiz.why: A strong evaluation looks at both strengths and limitations, using evidence.

quiz.why: The key advantage of democracy is that it provides a process by which mistakes can be corrected.

questions.q: Democracy allows citizens to examine decision-making. This is called
questions.why: Citizens' right to examine how decisions are made is called transparency.

questions.q: Which outcome means people accept the government as their own?
questions.why: Legitimacy means people accept the government as their own.

questions.q: Democracy is based on
questions.why: Democracy is based on political equality, with each person having one vote of equal value.

questions.why: Democracies have been less successful in reducing economic inequality.

options: Both true; R does not explain A

A fixed community should always rule

questions.why: The difference is 5.9 − 5.5 = 0.4 percentage points, which is small.

school-c10-social-c.title: Class 10 Social Science — Part C (Economics, Revision)

courses.title: Ch 1 · Development
courses.summary: What development means to different people, why income is important but not enough, how countries and states are compared using per capita income, IMR, literacy and HDI, and why development must be sustainable.
outcomes: Learners can explain why different people have different and even conflicting development goals
Learners can calculate average (per capita) income and explain its limits
Learners can interpret IMR, literacy rate, net attendance ratio and the HDI
Learners can explain sustainability of development with examples

scenes.text: A landless labourer wants more days of work and better wages.
A city girl wants as much freedom as her brother. A factory owner wants more electricity.

steps.title: Different goals, conflicting goals
steps.body:
People have different developmental goals depending on their life situations:
- **Landless rural labourers:** more days of work, better wages; local school for children; no social discrimination.
- **Prosperous farmers of Punjab:** assured high family income through higher support prices and hard-working cheap labourers.
- **Farmers dependent on rain:** more days of work; better irrigation.
- **Rural landowning family:** settle their children in cities.
- **An urban unemployed youth:** a good job.
- **A girl from a rich urban family:** as much freedom as her brother; freedom to decide what to do in life; study abroad.
- **An adivasi from Narmada valley:** protection of livelihood and forests.

Goals can **conflict**: to get more electricity, industrialists may want more dams, but this may submerge the land and disrupt the lives of people who are displaced – such as tribals. What may be development for one may not be development for another.

steps.title: Income and other goals
steps.body: People desire **regular work, better wages, decent prices** for crops – i.e. more income. But besides income, people also seek things like **equal treatment, freedom, security, respect of others** and dislike discrimination. Money cannot buy all goods and services needed for a good life – e.g. a pollution-free environment, unadulterated medicines, protection from infectious diseases. Non-material things matter: e.g. if women are given jobs, their dignity in the household and society increases; a safe and secure environment may allow more women to take up jobs. **Overall development** combines material and non-material goals.

steps.title: Solved example: Show how development goals can conflict, with an example (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Goal A:** industrialists want more electricity → more dams.

**Step 2 – Goal B:** people living in the valley (e.g. adivasis) want to protect land, forests and livelihood.

**Step 3 – Conflict:** the dam fulfils A but displaces B – development for one is destruction for another.

steps.title: Solved example: Why is income not the only goal of development? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** People also want freedom, equality, security and respect.

**Step 2:** Some goods – clean air, safe medicines, protection from disease – cannot be bought individually.

**Step 3:** Example: a woman's paid job raises income and her dignity; safety enables more women to work.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming everyone defines development the same way.
- Writing that money can buy all needs – collective goods like a clean environment cannot be bought individually.

activity.prompt: Match the person with a likely development goal
pairs: More days of work and better wages

quiz.q: Development goals of people are
quiz.why: Different people have different life situations, so their development goals differ and may even conflict.

quiz.q: Which is a non-material goal?
quiz.why: Freedom and respect are non-material goals. Higher wages, a bigger house and more crops are material.

quiz.q: A dam that displaces people shows
quiz.why: A dam may help some people with power or irrigation but displace others, so goals conflict.

quiz.q: Which cannot be bought individually with money?
quiz.why: A pollution-free environment is a collective good and cannot be bought by one person with money.

quiz.q: Overall development combines
quiz.why: Overall development includes both material and non-material goals.

lessons.title: National development and per capita income

scenes.text: Two islands each have five people and an average income of ₹10,000.
On one island, one person earns almost everything; on the other, all earn about the same.

steps.title: Comparing countries
steps.body:
National development means thinking about **what is fair and just for all**. For comparison, **income** is considered one of the most important attributes – countries with higher income are more developed.

**Average income** = total income of the country ÷ total population. It is also called **per capita income**.

The **World Bank** uses per capita income to classify countries in its **World Development Report**: high-income (rich) countries and low-income countries, with thresholds revised every year. India is in the low-middle income category. Rich countries, excluding countries of the Middle East and certain other small countries, are generally called **developed countries**.

**Limitation:** averages hide disparities – two countries with the same average income may have very unequal distributions.

steps.title: Solved example: Calculate average income (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Data:** Country X – five citizens earn ₹9,000, ₹10,500, ₹10,000, ₹9,500, ₹11,000. Country Y – ₹1,000, ₹1,000, ₹1,000, ₹1,000, ₹46,000.

**Step 1 – X total:** 9,000 + 10,500 + 10,000 + 9,500 + 11,000 = ₹50,000 → average = 50,000 ÷ 5 = **₹10,000**.

**Step 2 – Y total:** 4 × 1,000 + 46,000 = ₹50,000 → average = **₹10,000**.

**Step 3 – Conclusion:** same averages, but X is more equitable; most people in Y are poor. Average income alone can mislead.

steps.title: Solved example: Per capita income of a state (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Data:** total income ₹6,00,000 crore; population 3 crore.

**Step 1:** Per capita income = 6,00,000 crore ÷ 3 crore.

**Step 2:** = **₹2,00,000** per person per year.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dividing population by income instead of income by population.
- Thinking a high average means everyone is well-off – check **distribution**.
- Quoting old World Bank thresholds as permanent – they are **revised annually**.

activity.prompt: A country has a total income of ₹50 lakh crore and a population of 125 crore. Find per capita income in ₹.

quiz.q: Per capita income is
quiz.why: Per capita income is the average income, which is total income divided by population.

quiz.q: The World Bank classifies countries using
quiz.why: The World Bank classifies countries using per capita income, in its World Development Report.

quiz.q: The main limitation of averages is that they
quiz.why: The main limitation of averages is that they hide disparities, since they do not show how income is distributed.

quiz.q: Total income ₹1,000 crore, population 50 lakh. Per capita income?
quiz.why: Per capita income = total income ÷ population. ₹1,000 crore = ₹1,00,00,00,000 (10¹⁰) and 50 lakh = 50,00,000 (5 × 10⁶), so 10¹⁰ ÷ (5 × 10⁶) = ₹2,000 per person.

quiz.q: National development should consider
options: what is fair and just for all
quiz.why: National development should aim at what is fair and just for all, not only the rich.

scenes.text: A baby born in Kerala has a much better chance of surviving its first year than one in some richer states.
Health care and education, not just income, make the difference.

steps.title: Beyond income
steps.body:
- **Infant Mortality Rate (IMR):** the number of children who die before the age of one year as a proportion of **1,000 live children born** in that particular year.
- **Literacy rate:** the proportion of literate population in the **7 years and above** age group.
- **Net Attendance Ratio:** total number of children of age group **14 and 15 years** attending school as a percentage of total number of children in the same age group.

NCERT compares **Haryana, Kerala and Bihar**: Haryana has the highest per capita income, Bihar the lowest; yet **Kerala has a much lower IMR** and higher literacy, because of adequate basic health and educational facilities. Money cannot buy all goods and services; **public facilities** (health, education, PDS) provided collectively are often cheaper and better. Kerala and Himachal Pradesh show how public provision raises human development; a well-functioning **Public Distribution System (PDS)** improves nutrition.

**Body Mass Index (BMI):** weight in kg ÷ (height in m)². A BMI below 18.5 suggests undernourishment; above 25 overweight (adult values).

steps.title: Human Development Index
steps.body: The **Human Development Report** published by **UNDP** compares countries based on **educational levels** of people, their **health status** and **per capita income**. The HDI uses: **life expectancy at birth** (average expected length of life of a person at the time of birth), **mean years of schooling** of people aged 25 and above, **expected years of schooling** for children entering school, and **gross national income per capita** in PPP (purchasing power parity, US$). Sri Lanka, for example, ranks above India in HDI, though it is a much smaller country.

steps.title: Solved example: Calculate IMR (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Data:** in a district, 25,000 live births in a year; 750 infants died before age one.

**Step 1 – Formula:** IMR = (infant deaths ÷ live births) × 1,000.

**Step 2 – Calculate:** (750 ÷ 25,000) × 1,000 = **30 per 1,000 live births**.

steps.title: Solved example: Calculate BMI and interpret (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Data:** an adult weighs 45 kg, height 1.6 m.

**Step 1:** BMI = 45 ÷ (1.6 × 1.6) = 45 ÷ 2.56 ≈ **17.6**.

**Step 2:** Below 18.5 → **undernourished**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Defining IMR per 100 births – it is **per 1,000 live births**.
- Taking literacy for all ages – it is for **7 years and above**.
- Saying HDI is published by the World Bank – it is **UNDP**.

activity.prompt: A state records 18,000 live births and 360 infant deaths in a year. What is its IMR (per 1,000 live births)?

quiz.q: IMR measures deaths of children before age
quiz.why: The infant mortality rate (IMR) counts deaths of children before they reach the age of one year.

quiz.q: Literacy rate is measured for age group
quiz.why: The literacy rate is measured for the population aged 7 years and above.

quiz.q: Net Attendance Ratio is for children aged
quiz.why: The Net Attendance Ratio is for children aged 14 and 15.

quiz.q: HDI is published by
quiz.why: The Human Development Index is published by UNDP.

quiz.q: Why does Kerala have low IMR?
options: Adequate basic health and education facilities
quiz.why: Kerala has a low IMR because it has adequate basic health and education facilities.

scenes.text: Gurpreet's family tube well in Punjab has to be dug deeper every few years.
His teacher compares groundwater and crude oil – both can run out if over-used.

steps.title: Why sustainability matters
steps.body:
Even when development raises income, it may not be **sustainable** – it may not continue for future generations.

- **Groundwater:** overuse is a serious problem; NCERT notes that about one-third of the country is overusing groundwater reserves; in many areas (Punjab, western UP, hard-rock plateaus of central and south India, Rajasthan, Gujarat, coastal areas) the water table has fallen.
- **Non-renewable resources** like crude oil get exhausted after use; at present rates known reserves will last a limited number of years (NCERT presents a table of reserves).
- **Environmental degradation** does not respect state or national boundaries; it is a global concern.
- Sustainable development means meeting present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs. Scientists, economists, philosophers and social scientists are working together on it.

steps.title: Solved example: Why is groundwater overuse a sustainability issue? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Renewable but limited:** groundwater is replenished by rain, but slowly.

**Step 2 – Overuse:** when extraction exceeds recharge, the water table falls.

**Step 3 – Future:** future generations and farms lose access – development is not sustainable.

steps.title: Solved example: Crude oil reserves of 1,200 million barrels; extraction 60 million barrels per year. How many years will they last? (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Formula:** years = reserves ÷ annual extraction.

**Step 2:** 1,200 ÷ 60 = **20 years** (if no new reserves are found).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling groundwater non-renewable – it is renewable, but **overuse** makes it unsustainable.
- Thinking environmental damage stays within one state – it is a **global** issue.

statements.s: Sustainable development considers future generations.
Groundwater can never be overused.
Crude oil is a renewable resource.
Environmental degradation respects national boundaries.

quiz.q: Sustainable development means
options: meeting present needs without harming future needs
quiz.why: Sustainable development means meeting present needs without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs.

quiz.q: Groundwater is
quiz.why: Groundwater is renewable, but it can be overused if it is withdrawn faster than it is recharged.

quiz.q: Crude oil reserves 600 million barrels, use 30 million per year. Years left?
quiz.why: Years left = reserves ÷ yearly use = 600 ÷ 30 = 20 years.

quiz.q: Environmental degradation is
quiz.why: Environmental degradation crosses borders, so it is a global concern.

quiz.q: Which region has seen a falling water table?
quiz.why: Punjab has a falling water table due to over-use of groundwater for irrigation.

questions.q: Per capita income is also called
questions.why: Per capita income is also called average income.

questions.q: IMR is expressed per
questions.why: IMR is expressed per 1,000 live births.

questions.q: HDI is published by
questions.why: The HDI is published by UNDP.

questions.q: Which is a non-material aspect of development?
questions.why: Security and respect are non-material aspects of development.

questions.q: Literacy rate refers to population aged
questions.why: The literacy rate refers to the population aged 7 years and above.

questions.q: Which state is noted for low IMR due to public health and education?
questions.why: Kerala is noted for a low IMR due to its public health and education facilities.

questions.q: Assertion: Average income may hide disparities. Reason: Two countries with equal averages can have very different distributions.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. Two countries may have the same average income but very different distributions, so averages can hide disparities.

questions.q: Assertion: Higher income always ensures better health. Reason: Kerala has lower per capita income than Haryana but lower IMR.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Higher income does not always ensure better health, so A is false. Kerala has a lower per capita income than Haryana but a lower IMR, so R is true and shows A is false.

questions.q: Case: A dam brings electricity to cities but submerges tribal villages. This illustrates
questions.why: A dam that gives electricity to cities but submerges tribal villages shows how development goals can conflict.

questions.q: Which component is part of HDI?
questions.why: HDI uses life expectancy at birth, years of schooling and per capita income.

questions.q: Five people earn ₹2,000, ₹4,000, ₹6,000, ₹8,000 and ₹30,000. Average income?
In the data above, how many people earn less than the average?
questions.why: Four of the five people earn less than ₹10,000, which shows that the average can be misleading.

questions.q: A district has 40,000 live births and 1,000 infant deaths. IMR?
An adult is 1.5 m tall and weighs 54 kg. BMI and status?
questions.why: BMI = weight ÷ height² = 54 ÷ 2.25 = 24, which is within the normal range of 18.5 to 25.

questions.q: Why are public facilities important for development?
options: It is cheaper to provide collective services like health and schools than for each to buy them
questions.why: It is cheaper and more effective to provide collective services like health and schools through the public than for each person to buy them.

questions.q: Net Attendance Ratio is for age group
questions.why: The Net Attendance Ratio is measured for children aged 14 and 15.

courses.title: Ch 2 · Sectors of the Indian Economy
courses.summary: Primary, secondary and tertiary sectors; measuring GDP without double counting; how sector shares changed in India; underemployment and MGNREGA; organised vs unorganised and public vs private sectors.
outcomes: Learners can classify activities into primary, secondary and tertiary sectors
Learners can compute GDP using final goods and avoid double counting
Learners can explain the rise of the tertiary sector and disguised unemployment
Learners can compare organised/unorganised and public/private sectors

story.title: From cotton to shirt to shop

scenes.text: A farmer grows cotton (primary), a mill turns it into cloth (secondary), and a transporter and shop sell the shirt (tertiary).
Economists add only the value of the final shirt to GDP.

steps.title: The three sectors
steps.body:
- **Primary sector:** activities that directly use natural resources – agriculture, dairy, fishing, forestry, mining. Also called the **agriculture and related sector**.
- **Secondary sector:** natural products are changed into other forms through manufacturing – e.g. making cloth from cotton, sugar from cane, bricks from earth. Also called the **industrial sector**.
- **Tertiary sector:** activities that help development of primary and secondary sectors; they don't produce goods but are an aid – transport, storage, communication, banking, trade. Also called the **service sector**. It also includes services like teachers, doctors, washermen, barbers, lawyers, and IT-based services (internet cafés, ATM booths, call centres, software companies).

steps.title: Comparing sectors: GDP
steps.body:
Only **final goods and services** are counted, because the value of final goods already includes the value of all **intermediate goods** used to make them; counting both would be **double counting**.

**Gross Domestic Product (GDP):** the value of all final goods and services produced within a country during a particular year. It shows how big the economy is. In India, GDP is measured by a central government ministry with the help of state governments and union territories (the **Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation**).

**Historical change:** in the early stages of development, the primary sector was most important; as farming methods improved and surplus grew, the secondary sector became important; over the past 100 years in developed countries the tertiary sector has become the most important in terms of total production and employment.

steps.title: Solved example: Avoiding double counting (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Data:** a farmer sells wheat to a flour mill for ₹8; the mill sells flour to a biscuit company for ₹10; the company sells biscuits for ₹60.

**Step 1 – Identify final good:** biscuits (sold to consumers).

**Step 2 – Count only final value:** ₹60 (it already includes wheat ₹8 and flour ₹10).

**Step 3 – Wrong method:** 8 + 10 + 60 = ₹78 – double counting.

steps.title: Solved example: Classify activities (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Primary:** fisherman catching fish, a miner extracting coal.

**Step 2 – Secondary:** a potter making pots, a sugar mill.

**Step 3 – Tertiary:** a courier delivering parcels, a bank lending money, a teacher.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting intermediate goods in GDP – causes **double counting**.
- Classifying a potter as primary – making pots from clay is **manufacturing (secondary)**.
- Forgetting that GDP is for a **year** and **within the country**.

activity.prompt: Sort the activity into a sector

quiz.q: The tertiary sector is also called
quiz.why: The tertiary sector is also called the service sector.

quiz.q: GDP counts
quiz.why: GDP counts only the value of final goods and services, to avoid counting the same value twice.

quiz.q: Making sugar from sugarcane is a
quiz.why: Making sugar from sugarcane is manufacturing, so it is a secondary activity.

quiz.q: Who measures GDP in India?
options: A central government ministry with states and UTs
quiz.why: In India GDP is measured by a central government ministry, with the help of state and UT governments.

quiz.q: Wheat ₹8 → flour ₹10 → bread ₹50 (final). Value added to GDP?
quiz.why: Only the value of the final good, bread, is counted in GDP, which is ₹50. The earlier values are already included in it.

lessons.title: Rise of the tertiary sector; where are the jobs?

scenes.text: Ira's cousin works for an IT company; output in services has grown fastest.
But her grandparents' village still has most people working on farms.

steps.title: Why the tertiary sector grew
steps.body:
1. **Basic services** (hospitals, schools, post and telegraph, police, courts, municipal corporations, defence, transport, banks, insurance) – the government must provide these in any country.
2. Development of agriculture and industry leads to development of services like **transport, trade, storage**.
3. As income rises, people demand more services – **eating out, tourism, shopping, private hospitals, private schools, professional training**.
4. New services based on **information and communication technology** have grown rapidly.

But not all of the tertiary sector is growing well – it includes highly skilled, well-paid jobs and also a large number of small, poorly-paid workers (small shopkeepers, repair persons, transport persons) with little choice of jobs.

steps.title: Jobs and underemployment
steps.body:
The tertiary sector became the largest producing sector in India, replacing the primary sector. However, the **primary sector continues to be the largest employer** – more than half of workers were in it in early years and still a large share (NCERT data). The secondary and tertiary sectors did not create enough jobs; their share in employment rose much less than their share in production.

**Underemployment / disguised unemployment:** people appear to be working but all are made to work less than their potential. E.g. a family of five works on a small plot that needs only two people; the extra three are disguisedly unemployed – removing them would not reduce output. It is also found in services in urban areas (casual workers searching for daily work, street vendors).

**How to create more jobs:** loans for irrigation (wells) and better cultivation; dams and canals; transport and storage (roads, cold storage); local industries for processing (dal mills, honey collection); expanding education and health services; tourism; regional craft industry.

**MGNREGA 2005:** the **Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005** guarantees **100 days of employment in a year** to every rural household that demands work in many districts of India. If the government fails to provide work, it must give **unemployment allowance** to the people. Work that increases production from land is given preference. One-third of the proposed jobs are reserved for women.

steps.title: Solved example: Identify disguised unemployment (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Data:** a farm of 2 hectares needs 3 workers; 6 family members work on it and output is 40 quintals. If 3 leave for jobs in town, output stays 40 quintals.

**Step 1 – Test:** does output fall when some workers leave? No.

**Step 2 – Conclusion:** the 3 extra workers were **disguisedly unemployed**.

**Step 3 – Solution:** create other work – processing units, irrigation projects, services.

steps.title: Solved example: Sector shares (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Data:** GDP = ₹100 lakh crore; primary ₹18, secondary ₹27, tertiary ₹55 lakh crore.

**Step 1:** Shares = 18%, 27%, 55%.

**Step 2:** Tertiary is the largest producing sector; primary's share in output is smallest even though it employs the most people.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the tertiary sector is the largest **employer** – it is the largest **producer**; primary remains the largest employer.
- Writing MGNREGA guarantees 200 days – it guarantees **100 days** per rural household per year.

activity.prompt: Complete the MGNREGA facts
activity.text: MGNREGA was passed in ___ . It guarantees ___ days of work per year to every rural household that demands it. If work is not given, the government pays an unemployment ___ .

quiz.q: Disguised unemployment means
options: more people work than needed so output does not fall if some leave
quiz.why: In disguised unemployment more people work than needed, so output would not fall if some left.

quiz.q: The largest employer in India remains the
quiz.why: The primary sector still employs the largest number of people in India.

quiz.q: Which is a reason for growth of services?
options: Rising incomes increase demand for services
quiz.why: As incomes rise, people demand more services like education, health and travel, so services grow.

quiz.q: MGNREGA guarantees work for
quiz.why: MGNREGA guarantees 100 days of work to rural households that ask for it.

quiz.q: Which creates jobs in rural areas?
quiz.why: Cold storage and better roads create jobs in rural areas by supporting farm-based processing and trade.

scenes.text: Kanta works in an office: fixed hours, paid leave, provident fund.
Kamal is a daily-wage labourer: no fixed work, no leave, no security.

steps.title: Organised vs unorganised
steps.body:
- **Organised sector:** enterprises or places of work where the terms of employment are **regular** and people have assured work. They are **registered** by the government and follow its rules and regulations (Factories Act, Minimum Wages Act, Payment of Gratuity Act, Shops and Establishments Act). Workers get **job security**, fixed working hours, overtime pay, paid leave, payment during holidays, provident fund, gratuity, medical benefits, pension.
- **Unorganised sector:** small and scattered units largely **outside government control**. Rules exist but are not followed. Jobs are low-paid and often not regular; no provision for overtime, paid leave, holidays, sick leave; employment is not secure – people can be asked to leave without reason. Many work in their own small businesses or in small-scale industry.

**Protecting unorganised workers:** in rural areas – landless agricultural labourers, small and marginal farmers, sharecroppers, artisans (weavers, blacksmiths, carpenters, goldsmiths); in urban areas – workers in small-scale industry, casual workers in construction, trade and transport, street vendors, head-load workers, garment makers, rag pickers. Many are from SC, ST and backward communities, who face social discrimination too. The government can fix minimum wages and working hours, provide cheap loans, storage and marketing for small farmers, and support small-scale industries with raw material procurement and marketing.

steps.title: Public vs private sector
steps.body:
- **Public sector:** the **government owns** most of the assets and provides all the services – e.g. railways, post office. Its purpose is not just profit but **welfare**.
- **Private sector:** ownership of assets and delivery of services is in the hands of **private individuals or companies** – e.g. Tata Iron and Steel Company Limited (TISCO), Reliance Industries Limited (RIL). Activities are guided by the motive to earn **profits**.

**Why the government provides some services:** some things are needed by society but the private sector cannot provide them at reasonable cost – roads, bridges, railways, harbours, electricity, dams (huge spending). Some activities need government support – e.g. electricity at cost private companies may not charge; buying food grains from farmers at a fair price and selling at a lower price in ration shops (subsidy). Also: running proper schools and quality education, health facilities, nutrition (India's child malnutrition and high IMR call for government action – NCERT data).

steps.title: Solved example: Compare the organised and unorganised sectors (4 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Registration:** organised – registered, follows laws; unorganised – largely outside government control.

**Step 2 – Job security:** organised – secure, regular; unorganised – irregular, can be dismissed any time.

**Step 3 – Benefits:** organised – paid leave, PF, medical benefits; unorganised – few or none.

**Step 4 – Example:** government office clerk vs daily-wage construction worker.

steps.title: Solved example: Why can't all services be left to the private sector? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Huge costs:** roads, dams, railways need large investment; private firms may charge high prices.

**Step 2 – Welfare:** subsidised ration and electricity for the poor are not profitable.

**Step 3 – Basic needs:** health and education for all require government provision.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying organised = public and unorganised = private – a private company can be **organised** (registered, follows rules).
- Calling the public sector profit-driven – its main aim is **welfare**.

activity.prompt: Organised or unorganised?

items.text: Bank clerk with PF and paid leave
Factory worker in a registered unit with fixed hours

quiz.q: The organised sector is characterised by
options: registered units and regular terms of employment
quiz.why: The organised sector has registered units and regular terms of employment.

quiz.q: Which is a private sector company?
quiz.why: TISCO (Tata Iron and Steel Company) is a private sector company. Indian Railways and India Post are public sector.

quiz.q: The main aim of the public sector is
quiz.why: The main aim of the public sector is public welfare, not just profit.

quiz.q: Which law protects organised workers?
quiz.why: The Factories Act protects the rights and safety of organised sector workers.

quiz.q: Which group is part of the unorganised sector?
quiz.why: Rag pickers have irregular work and no job security, so they belong to the unorganised sector.

scenes.text: You are a district planner with ₹50 crore to create jobs.
Should you build a dam, cold storage, or a call centre?

steps.title: How to approach policy questions
steps.body:
- Identify the **sector** affected and the **type of unemployment** (open, disguised, seasonal).
- Suggest **job-creating investments** that link sectors (irrigation → more crops → processing → transport → trade).
- Mention protection for **unorganised** workers (minimum wages, loans, social security).
- Use MGNREGA as an example of a **right to work**.

steps.title: Solved example: Case: A district has rain-fed farms and long idle months (4 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Diagnosis:** seasonal and disguised unemployment in the primary sector.

**Step 2 – Primary:** build wells/check dams so a second crop is possible.

**Step 3 – Secondary/tertiary:** cold storage, dal mills, roads to markets create non-farm jobs.

**Step 4 – Safety net:** MGNREGA work on water conservation in lean months.

steps.title: Solved example: Case: A garment unit pays below minimum wage and fires workers without notice (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** It behaves as an unorganised-sector unit – rules not followed.

**Step 2:** Government should register and inspect such units, enforce minimum wages and job security.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Recommending only big factories – rural employment often grows faster through irrigation, storage and processing.
- Ignoring how sectors depend on one another.

a.text: District X: 70% of workers on small farms, many idle half the year. Where do you invest first?

choices.feedback: Links primary to secondary and tertiary sectors.

choices.label: Nothing more
choices.feedback: Without storage and markets, extra produce may rot or sell cheap.

c.text: Jobs for the rural poor barely grow. Think about linking sectors and reducing disguised unemployment.

d.text: Employment and incomes grow across all three sectors – a sound plan. Add MGNREGA works for the lean season.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Money and Credit
courses.summary: Money as a medium of exchange, modern forms of money and bank deposits, how banks lend, terms of credit, formal and informal sources of loans in India, and self-help groups for the poor.
outcomes: Learners can explain double coincidence of wants and why money solves it
Learners can describe currency and demand deposits as modern money
Learners can analyse terms of credit and calculate interest and repayment
Learners can compare formal and informal credit and explain SHGs

lessons.title: Money as a medium of exchange; modern forms of money

scenes.text: A shoe-maker wants wheat. A wheat farmer wants cloth, not shoes.
Without money, the shoe-maker must find someone who has wheat AND wants shoes.

steps.title: Why money?
steps.body:
In a **barter system**, goods are directly exchanged without money. It requires a **double coincidence of wants** – what one person desires to sell is exactly what the other wishes to buy. This is rare. **Money** acts as an intermediate in the exchange process – a **medium of exchange** – eliminating the need for double coincidence.

Earlier forms: grains and cattle, then metallic coins (gold, silver, copper). Modern forms: **paper notes and coins** (currency) and **deposits with banks**.

steps.title: Currency and deposits
steps.body:
- **Currency:** in India, the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** issues currency notes on behalf of the central government. Currency is accepted as a medium of exchange because it is authorised by the government; no individual can refuse to accept the rupee in settling transactions (legal tender).
- **Deposits with banks:** people deposit extra cash in bank accounts and earn interest. Since money can be withdrawn on demand, these are called **demand deposits**. A **cheque** is a paper instructing the bank to pay a specific amount from the person's account to the person in whose name the cheque is made. Demand deposits share the essential features of money; payments can also be made digitally (UPI, debit cards, net banking).

steps.title: Solved example: Explain double coincidence of wants with an example (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Definition:** both parties must agree to sell and buy each other's goods.

**Step 2 – Example:** a weaver wants rice; a rice farmer wants a plough, not cloth – no exchange is possible.

**Step 3 – Money's role:** the weaver sells cloth for money to anyone and buys rice with money – exchange is easy.

steps.title: Solved example: Why are demand deposits considered money? (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** They can be withdrawn on demand and used for payments via cheques or digital transfers.

**Step 2:** So they work as a medium of exchange without using cash.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the central government prints and issues notes directly – the **RBI** issues them on behalf of the government.
- Calling demand deposits “loans” – they are **deposits** that the bank owes to the depositor.

statements.s: Barter requires double coincidence of wants.
The RBI issues currency notes on behalf of the central government.
A cheque is a loan from the bank.
statements.why: It is an instruction to pay from one's account.

statements.s: Demand deposits can be withdrawn on demand.

quiz.q: Money solves the problem of
quiz.why: Money solves the problem of the double coincidence of wants, since it acts as a medium of exchange.

quiz.q: Currency notes in India are issued by
quiz.why: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) issues currency notes on behalf of the central government.

quiz.q: Deposits withdrawable on demand are
quiz.why: Deposits that can be withdrawn on demand are called demand deposits.

quiz.q: A cheque is
options: an instruction to the bank to pay a sum from the account
quiz.why: A cheque is a written instruction to the bank to pay a sum from the drawer's account.

quiz.q: No one in India can refuse the rupee because
options: it is authorised by the government
quiz.why: The rupee is authorised by the government, so no one in India can refuse it as a means of payment.

lessons.title: Loan activities of banks and terms of credit

scenes.text: A shoe manufacturer takes a loan, fulfils a big order, repays on time and profits.
A farmer borrows for crops, but the crop fails – he sells land to repay. Credit can help or trap.

steps.title: How banks lend
steps.body:
Banks keep only a **small proportion** of their deposits as cash (NCERT: about **15%**) to pay depositors who may withdraw on a given day. They use the major portion to **extend loans**. Banks charge a **higher interest rate on loans** than they pay on deposits; the difference is the main source of income for banks. Banks thus **mediate** between those who have surplus funds (depositors) and those in need (borrowers).

**Credit (loan)** is an agreement in which the lender supplies the borrower with money, goods or services in return for the promise of future payment. Credit can push income up (shoe manufacturer) or, when risk strikes, cause a **debt trap** – a situation where the borrower is pushed into a situation from which recovery is very painful (failed crop, sale of land).

steps.title: Terms of credit
steps.body:
Every loan agreement specifies:
- **Interest rate** the borrower must pay to the lender along with the principal.
- **Collateral:** an asset the borrower owns (land, building, vehicle, livestock, deposits) used as a **guarantee** until the loan is repaid. If the borrower fails to repay, the lender has the right to sell the asset.
- **Documentation** required (e.g. proof of income, address).
- **Mode of repayment** (instalments, lump sum).

Terms vary depending on the nature of the lender and borrower.

steps.title: Solved example: Simple interest (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Data:** loan ₹50,000 at 12% per annum simple interest for 2 years.

**Step 1 – Formula:** SI = P × R × T ÷ 100.

**Step 2 – Calculate:** 50,000 × 12 × 2 ÷ 100 = **₹12,000**.

**Step 3 – Total repayment:** 50,000 + 12,000 = **₹62,000**.

steps.title: Solved example: Formal vs informal cost (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Data:** ₹20,000 for 1 year – bank at 10% p.a. vs moneylender at 5% per month.

**Step 1 – Bank interest:** 20,000 × 10% = ₹2,000.

**Step 2 – Moneylender interest:** 5% × 12 = 60% p.a. → 20,000 × 60% = ₹12,000.

**Step 3 – Difference:** ₹10,000 more to the moneylender – high interest leaves less income for the borrower.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying banks keep most deposits as cash – they keep only a **small share (~15%)** and lend the rest.
- Treating collateral as interest – collateral is a **guarantee asset**, not a payment.
- Forgetting to convert monthly rates to annual (×12).

activity.prompt: A farmer borrows ₹30,000 at 3% per month simple interest for 6 months. How much interest does he pay (₹)?

quiz.q: Banks' main source of income is
options: difference between interest on loans and deposits
quiz.why: Banks earn mainly from the difference between the interest charged on loans and the interest paid on deposits.

quiz.q: Collateral is
options: an asset used as a guarantee for a loan
quiz.why: Collateral is an asset that the borrower pledges as a guarantee against a loan.

quiz.q: A debt trap occurs when
options: repayment becomes very painful, often requiring sale of assets
quiz.why: In a debt trap, repayment becomes so painful that the borrower may have to sell assets to repay.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a term of credit?
quiz.why: Terms of credit include the interest rate, collateral, documentation and mode of repayment. The colour of the bank is irrelevant.

quiz.q: Loan ₹10,000 at 15% p.a. for 1 year. Interest?

lessons.title: Formal and informal sector credit in India

scenes.text: Swati, a small farmer, cannot get a bank loan because she has no land papers.
The village moneylender lends quickly – at 5% a month.

steps.title: Formal vs informal sources
steps.body:
- **Formal sector loans:** from **banks and cooperatives**. The **RBI supervises** their functioning: banks must maintain a minimum cash balance, the RBI checks that they give loans not just to profit-making businesses and traders but also to small cultivators, small-scale industries and small borrowers. Banks submit periodic information to the RBI on lending, to whom, at what interest rate.
- **Informal sector loans:** from **moneylenders, traders, employers, relatives and friends**. There is **no organisation that supervises** their credit activities; they lend at whatever interest rate they choose; there is no one to stop unfair means of getting money back. Interest is often very high; a large part of earnings goes to repaying loans.

**Who borrows from where:** NCERT data show that richer urban households take most loans from formal sources, whereas poorer households depend largely on informal sources. Reasons: lack of collateral, documentation; banks are absent or far in rural areas; informal lenders know borrowers personally and lend without collateral, even when earlier loans are unpaid.

**Need:** cheap and affordable credit is crucial for development – formal credit should expand to reach everyone, especially the poor; it should also be distributed more equally.

steps.title: Solved example: Why do the poor depend on informal lenders? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Collateral:** they lack land or assets to pledge.

**Step 2 – Documentation and access:** banks need papers; branches may be far away.

**Step 3 – Personal ties:** moneylenders know them and lend quickly without collateral – but at high interest.

steps.title: Solved example: Why is the RBI's supervision important? (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** It ensures banks keep a minimum cash balance, protecting depositors.

**Step 2:** It ensures loans reach small farmers and small industries, not only big businesses.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling cooperatives informal – they are **formal** lenders.
- Saying the RBI supervises moneylenders – informal lenders are **not supervised**.

activity.prompt: Formal or informal source?

quiz.q: Who supervises formal lending in India?
quiz.why: The RBI supervises formal lending by banks, making sure they give loans to different groups.

quiz.q: Which is an informal source of credit?
quiz.why: A moneylender is an informal source of credit. Banks, cooperative societies and RRBs are formal sources.

quiz.q: Poor households rely more on
quiz.why: Poor households depend more on informal sources of credit because they have less access to banks.

quiz.q: Informal lenders often
quiz.why: Informal lenders often charge very high interest and are not supervised by anyone.

quiz.q: Cheap credit is important because
options: it helps people start and expand productive activities
quiz.why: Cheap credit helps people start and expand productive activities, which supports development.

scenes.text: Rihana joined a self-help group of 15 women who save ₹100 a month each.
After two years the group got a bank loan; she bought a sewing machine.

steps.title: How SHGs work
steps.body:
In recent years people have tried new ways of providing loans to the poor – organising rural poor, especially **women**, into small **self-help groups (SHGs)** and pooling their savings.

- A typical SHG has **15–20 members**, usually from one neighbourhood, who meet and save regularly. Saving per member varies from ₹25 to ₹100 or more depending on ability.
- Members can take small loans from the group itself to meet their needs; the group charges interest on these loans (still less than the moneylender).
- After a year or two, if the group is regular in savings, it becomes **eligible for a bank loan**, sanctioned in the name of the group, to create self-employment opportunities (e.g. buying raw material, sewing machines, livestock, handlooms).
- Most important decisions (savings, loans, purpose, amount, interest, repayment) are taken by group members; the group is responsible for repayment. Any non-repayment is followed up seriously by other members – so banks are willing to lend even without collateral.
- SHGs help borrowers overcome the problem of **lack of collateral**, give **timely loans** at reasonable interest, and are building blocks of organisation of the rural poor; they help women become financially self-reliant and discuss social issues (health, nutrition, domestic violence).

**Grameen Bank of Bangladesh**, started in the 1970s, is a success story of reaching the poor; its founder **Professor Muhammad Yunus** received the **Nobel Peace Prize in 2006**.

steps.title: Solved example: How do SHGs solve the collateral problem? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** The loan is given to the group, not one individual.

**Step 2:** Group savings and peer pressure ensure repayment – members follow up defaults.

**Step 3:** So banks lend without individual collateral.

steps.title: Solved example: SHG savings (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Data:** 18 members save ₹100 per month for 24 months.

**Step 1:** Monthly saving = 18 × 100 = ₹1,800.

**Step 2:** Total = 1,800 × 24 = **₹43,200** (before interest).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing that SHG loans are given by moneylenders – they come from **group savings and banks**.
- Saying Muhammad Yunus founded an Indian bank – he founded the **Grameen Bank of Bangladesh**.

items: Small loans are given from the group's own savings
After 1–2 years of regular saving the group becomes eligible for a bank loan

quiz.why: A typical self-help group has 15–20 members, usually from the same neighbourhood.

quiz.why: Muhammad Yunus founded the Grameen Bank of Bangladesh and received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2006.

quiz.why: SHGs help poor people borrow without the collateral they would otherwise need.

quiz.why: Total savings = 12 members × ₹50 × 12 months = ₹7,200.

questions.why: SHGs usually have 15–20 members.

questions.why: Collateral is a guarantee against a loan that the lender can sell if the loan is not repaid.

questions.why: Banks keep about 15% of their deposits as cash, because only some depositors withdraw on any day.

questions.q: A debt trap is most likely when
questions.why: A debt trap is likely when crops fail after borrowing at high interest, since the borrower cannot repay.

questions.q: Assertion: Banks can lend without keeping all deposits as cash. Reason: Only a few depositors withdraw on any given day.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. Only a small share of depositors withdraw on a given day, so banks can lend most of the deposits.
