options: Both true; R does not explain A

questions.why: A woman without land who saves with neighbours and later gets a group loan is part of a self-help group.

options: A cheque is legal tender currency
A cheque instructs the bank to pay from the drawer's account

questions.q: Why do richer urban households take more formal loans?
options: They have collateral and documentation and live near banks
questions.why: Richer urban households have collateral and papers and live near banks, so they find it easy to take formal loans.

questions.q: Which is a key reason formal credit must expand?
options: Informal credit's high interest leaves borrowers with less income
questions.why: Informal credit carries high interest, which leaves borrowers with less income. So cheaper formal credit should expand.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Globalisation and the Indian Economy
courses.summary: How MNCs spread production across countries, how foreign trade integrates markets, what globalisation is and what made it possible (technology, liberalisation, WTO), its impact on India, and the struggle for fair globalisation.
outcomes: Learners can explain how MNCs interlink production across countries
Learners can describe how foreign trade integrates markets
Learners can explain the roles of technology, liberalisation and the WTO
Learners can evaluate the impact of globalisation on different groups in India

scenes.text: Aditya's phone was designed in one country, its chips made in another, and assembled in India.
This is how multinational corporations spread production.

steps.title: MNCs and interlinking production
steps.body:
A **multinational corporation (MNC)** is a company that owns or controls production in more than one nation. MNCs set up offices and factories in regions where they can get cheap labour and other resources, to reduce costs and earn greater profits.

**Factors MNCs consider:** closeness to markets; availability of skilled and unskilled labour at low cost; assured availability of other factors of production; government policies that look after their interests.

**Ways MNCs spread production:**
1. **Joint production** with local companies – the MNC provides money for additional investment (e.g. new machines) and the latest technology; the local company gets these benefits.
2. **Buying up local companies** and then expanding production – e.g. **Cargill Foods** (an American MNC) bought **Parakh Foods**, a small Indian company, and became a large producer of edible oil in India.
3. **Placing orders with small producers** – e.g. garments, footwear and sports items are produced by small producers around the world for large MNCs, which then sell under their own brand names.

**Investment:** money spent to buy assets such as land, buildings, machines; investment made by MNCs is **foreign investment**.

steps.title: Solved example: Explain three ways MNCs control production (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Joint production:** MNC + local firm; MNC brings money and technology.

**Step 2 – Buying local companies:** e.g. Cargill bought Parakh Foods and expanded.

**Step 3 – Orders to small producers:** small firms make garments/footwear sold under MNC brands.

steps.title: Solved example: Why would an MNC set up a call centre in India? (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Availability of English-speaking, educated youth at relatively low cost.

**Step 2:** Good communication infrastructure and supportive government policies.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling any big company an MNC – an MNC must own or control production in **more than one country**.
- Saying Parakh Foods bought Cargill – **Cargill bought Parakh**.

activity.prompt: Match the MNC strategy to the example
pairs: MNC provides machines and technology to a local firm
Garments made by small firms for big brands
Setting up factories close to customers

quiz.q: An MNC owns or controls production in
quiz.why: A multinational company owns or controls production in more than one nation.

quiz.q: Cargill Foods bought
quiz.why: Cargill Foods, an American MNC, bought Parakh Foods, an Indian company.

quiz.q: Investment made by MNCs is called
quiz.why: Money spent by MNCs to set up assets such as factories is called foreign investment.

quiz.q: Which factor attracts MNCs?
quiz.why: MNCs set up production where labour is cheap and skilled, and the market is nearby.

quiz.q: Placing orders with small producers lets MNCs
options: sell under their own brand names
quiz.why: By placing orders with small producers, MNCs get goods made cheaply and sell them under their own brand names.

lessons.title: Foreign trade and integration of markets

scenes.text: Indian toy shops filled with cheaper Chinese toys; local toy makers faced tough competition.
Buyers got more choice; sellers had to compete across borders.

steps.title: How trade integrates markets
steps.body:
For a long time foreign trade has been the main channel connecting countries. **Foreign trade creates an opportunity for producers to reach beyond domestic markets**; buyers get more choice of goods. With trade, goods travel from one market to another, prices of similar goods in two markets tend to become equal, and producers in two countries now compete closely despite being thousands of miles apart. Foreign trade thus results in **connecting/integration of markets** in different countries.

Example: Chinese toys imported into India – Indian buyers get more choice at lower prices; Chinese toy makers get a bigger market; Indian toy makers face competition and losses.

steps.title: Solved example: How does foreign trade integrate markets? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Producers sell beyond domestic markets; buyers choose from domestic and imported goods.

**Step 2:** Prices of similar goods in two markets tend to equalise.

**Step 3:** Producers in different countries compete directly – markets become connected.

steps.body:
**Step 1 – Gained:** Indian buyers (choice, lower prices); foreign producers (bigger market).

**Step 2 – Lost:** Indian toy makers – lower sales.

**Step 3 – Lesson:** trade benefits are uneven.

- Forgetting that integration means **competition across borders**.

lessons.title: What made globalisation possible: technology, liberalisation, WTO

scenes.text: In 1991 India changed its policies to allow more imports and foreign investment.
Meanwhile the internet and cheaper shipping made the world smaller.

steps.title: Globalisation and its drivers
steps.body:
**Globalisation** is the process of **rapid integration or interconnection between countries** – more goods and services, more investment and more technology moving between countries; to some extent people also move (for jobs, education).

**Factors:**
1. **Technology:** rapid improvement in transportation (containers lowered port costs and increased speed) and in **information and communication technology** – telecommunication, computers, internet, satellite links – allows services like design, accounts, call centres to be done remotely.
2. **Liberalisation of foreign trade and investment policy:** a **trade barrier** is a restriction on foreign trade – e.g. a **tax on imports** (tariff) or limits on quantity. After Independence, India put barriers to protect producers within the country. Around **1991**, the government decided that the time had come for Indian producers to compete with producers around the globe; barriers were removed to a large extent. Removing barriers or restrictions set by the government is **liberalisation**.
3. **World Trade Organisation (WTO):** its aim is to **liberalise international trade**; it establishes rules regarding international trade and sees that they are obeyed (over **160 member countries**). Though WTO is supposed to allow free trade for all, developed countries have unfairly retained trade barriers, while developing countries have been forced to remove theirs – e.g. developed countries like the US give large subsidies to their farmers, making their farm products cheaper.

steps.title: Solved example: What is liberalisation? Give two examples (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Definition:** removing barriers or restrictions set by the government on trade and investment.

**Step 2 – Example 1:** reducing import taxes so foreign goods can enter.

**Step 3 – Example 2:** allowing MNCs to invest and set up factories (India, from 1991).

steps.title: Solved example: Is the WTO fair? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Aim:** liberalise trade with common rules.

**Step 2 – Problem:** developed countries keep subsidies (e.g. US farm subsidies) while pressing developing countries to remove barriers.

**Step 3 – Judgement:** rules are not applied equally – fairness is questioned.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Equating globalisation with only trade – it also includes **investment, technology and people**.
- Dating India's liberalisation to 1947 – it began around **1991**.
- Saying WTO members follow rules equally – developed countries have retained barriers unfairly.

quiz.why: A tax on imports makes imported goods costlier, so it is a trade barrier.

quiz.why: Containers cut the cost of moving goods through ports.

lessons.title: Impact on India and the struggle for fair globalisation

scenes.text: Ravi started a small capacitor unit in 2001. After import duties fell, cheaper imports arrived.
His orders fell, and his workers lost jobs; meanwhile some Indian firms became global giants.

steps.title: Who gained, who lost
steps.body:
- **Consumers**, particularly the well-off in urban areas, gained greater choice, improved quality and lower prices of products (TVs, mobile phones, cars).
- **MNCs** increased investments in India in industries like cell phones, automobiles, electronics, soft drinks, fast food and services such as banking; new jobs were created; local companies supplying raw materials to MNCs prospered.
- **Top Indian companies** benefited: invested in new technology, raised standards, collaborated with foreign companies; some became **MNCs themselves** – e.g. **Tata Motors** (automobiles), **Infosys** (IT), **Ranbaxy** (medicines), **Asian Paints** (paints), **Sundaram Fasteners** (nuts and bolts).
- New opportunities for **services**, particularly IT.
- **Special Economic Zones (SEZs)** were set up with world-class facilities; companies there are exempt from taxes for an initial period. The government has also allowed **flexibility in labour laws**.
- **Losers:** small manufacturers hit by competition – e.g. batteries, capacitors, plastics, toys, tyres, dairy products, vegetable oil; many units shut down, workers lost jobs. Workers face uncertain employment – employers prefer flexible, temporary hiring; long hours, night shifts in the peak season, low pay (garment workers in exporting factories).

steps.title: Fair globalisation
steps.body: Globalisation should create opportunities for all and ensure its benefits are better shared. The **government** can play a major role: ensure labour laws are properly implemented and workers get their rights; support small producers to improve performance until they become strong enough to compete; use trade and investment barriers when necessary; negotiate at the WTO for fairer rules; align with other developing countries against domination of developed countries. **People's organisations** and campaigns have also influenced decisions on trade and investment at the WTO.

steps.title: Solved example: “Globalisation has not been equally beneficial.” Explain (4 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Gainers:** urban well-off consumers (choice, prices); top Indian companies (Tata Motors, Infosys became MNCs); skilled IT workers.

**Step 2 – Losers:** small producers (toys, batteries, capacitors, dairy) faced competition and closures.

**Step 3 – Workers:** flexible labour laws mean temporary jobs, long hours, low security.

**Step 4 – Conclusion:** benefits are concentrated; fair globalisation needs government and people's action.

steps.title: Solved example: What can the government do for fair globalisation? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Implement labour laws properly so workers get rights.

**Step 2:** Support small producers and use trade barriers when needed.

**Step 3:** Negotiate at WTO for fairer rules alongside other developing countries.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying SEZ firms pay normal taxes from the start – they get **tax exemption for an initial period**.
- Claiming all Indian producers gained – **small producers** were hit hard.

questions.q: A toy costs ₹200 in India and ₹120 in China. With an import tax of 50% on the Chinese price, its landed price in India (ignoring transport) is
questions.why: Import tax = 50% of 120 = ₹60, so the landed price is 120 + 60 = ₹180. It is still cheaper than the Indian toy at ₹200.

questions.q: In the case above, what import tax rate would make the Chinese toy cost exactly ₹200?
questions.why: We need 120 × (1 + t) = 200, so 1 + t = 1.667 and t ≈ 0.667, which is about 67%.

courses.title: Ch 5 · Consumer Rights
courses.summary: How consumers are exploited in the market, the rise of the consumer movement, the rights of consumers under India's consumer protection law, consumer commissions for redressal, and standardisation marks. (CBSE has treated this chapter as project work in recent years – check your current syllabus.)
outcomes: Learners can identify ways consumers are exploited
Learners can list consumer rights with examples
Learners can explain the three-tier redressal system and how to file a complaint
Learners can recognise ISI, Agmark and Hallmark and the role of consumer awareness
courses.note: CBSE has treated this chapter as project work in recent sessions; check the current syllabus

scenes.text: Neha weighs a "1 kg" packet of sugar at home – it is only 900 g.
The shopkeeper shrugs: "Take it or leave it."

steps.title: Forms of exploitation
steps.body:
We participate in markets both as **producers** and as **consumers**. Rules and regulations are needed to protect consumers because individual consumers are often in a weak position.

**Ways consumers are exploited:**
- **Underweight and undermeasurement** of goods.
- **Adulteration** – e.g. mixing cheap oil in edible oil, stones in grain.
- **Defective goods**; **high prices** above the maximum retail price (MRP).
- **False or incomplete information** – advertisements and labels that mislead.
- **Poor after-sales service**; **unsafe products** (e.g. faulty electrical appliances, expired medicines).
- **Large companies** with huge wealth, power and reach can manipulate the market and influence buyers through media.

steps.title: The consumer movement
steps.body:
The consumer movement arose out of **dissatisfaction** of consumers with unfair practices. In India it began as a **social force** to protect and promote consumers' interests against unethical and unfair trade practices; rampant food shortages, hoarding, black marketing and adulteration in the **1960s** gave birth to it in an organised form. Consumer groups wrote articles and held exhibitions. A major step was the **Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (COPRA)**, now replaced by the **Consumer Protection Act, 2019**, which also set up the **Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA)** and covers e-commerce.

**International:** **Consumers International** (earlier International Organisation of Consumers Unions) – in **1985** the UN adopted the **UN Guidelines for Consumer Protection**. **15 March** is **World Consumer Rights Day**; **24 December** is **National Consumers' Day** in India (the day the 1986 Act was enacted).

steps.title: Solved example: Identify the exploitation (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – A “1 litre” bottle has 900 ml:** undermeasurement.

**Step 2 – Chilli powder mixed with brick dust:** adulteration.

**Step 3 – Shop charges ₹25 for a ₹20 MRP item:** overcharging above MRP.

steps.title: Solved example: Why are consumers in a weak position? (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Individual buyers lack information and bargaining power compared with large sellers.

**Step 2:** Big companies can influence the market through media and advertising.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking COPRA 1986 is still the current law – it was replaced by the **Consumer Protection Act, 2019**.
- Mixing up the dates: **15 March** world day, **24 December** India's day.

quiz.why: The organised consumer movement in India arose in the 1960s, because of food shortages, hoarding, black marketing and adulteration.

quiz.why: Adulteration means mixing inferior or harmful substances into goods.

quiz.why: The Consumer Protection Act of 2019 is the present law, and it replaced COPRA 1986.

scenes.text: A pressure cooker with a faulty valve bursts in Aman's kitchen.
His sister reminds him: consumers have a right to safety – and to redressal.

steps.title: The rights
steps.body:
- **Right to safety:** protection against marketing of goods and services that are hazardous to life and property (e.g. pressure cookers need a safety valve; electrical goods and medicines must meet standards).
- **Right to be informed:** about the quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard and price of goods. Packets must show ingredients, price (MRP), batch number, date of manufacture, expiry date and address of the manufacturer. The **Right to Information Act (2005)** similarly gives citizens information about functions of government departments.
- **Right to choose:** any consumer who receives a service, whatever age, gender or nature of service, has the right to choose whether to continue to receive it. E.g. a shop cannot force you to buy a brand of toothpaste with a toothbrush you want; a gas dealer cannot force you to buy a stove with a connection.
- **Right to seek redressal:** against unfair trade practices and exploitation; compensation depending on the degree of damage.
- **Right to represent:** consumers can be represented in consumer commissions/forums.
- **Right to consumer education:** to acquire knowledge and skills to be an informed consumer.

**Duties of consumers:** check the quality, look for standardisation marks, ask for a **cash memo/bill**, read labels, file complaints for genuine grievances, form consumer awareness organisations.

steps.title: Solved example: Which right is violated? (4 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – A medicine strip has no expiry date:** right to be informed.

**Step 2 – A gas agency forces you to buy a stove:** right to choose.

**Step 3 – A helmet without standard mark cracks on minor impact:** right to safety.

**Step 4 – A shop refuses to replace a defective phone under warranty:** right to seek redressal.

steps.title: Solved example: Why should you insist on a bill? (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** It is proof of purchase – needed to file a complaint.

**Step 2:** It records price, date and seller details, preventing disputes.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing the right to choose with the right to be informed.
- Thinking only goods are covered – **services** (banking, telecom, hospitals, e-commerce) are covered too.

quiz.why: Printing MRP and expiry date gives information to consumers, so it is the right to be informed.

quiz.why: The right to seek redressal gives consumers a way to get compensation when they are exploited.

quiz.why: Consumers should ask for a cash memo (bill), since it is proof of purchase.

scenes.text: After a hospital's negligence harms his son, Reji's family files a complaint.
The commission orders compensation. Consumers can fight back.

steps.title: Three-tier quasi-judicial machinery
steps.body:
Under the consumer protection law, a three-tier **quasi-judicial** machinery exists at the **district, state and national** levels:
- **District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission** (district level)
- **State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission** (state level)
- **National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission** (national level, New Delhi)

Under the 2021 rules made under the 2019 Act, the District Commission deals with cases where the value of goods or services paid is **up to ₹50 lakh**, the State Commission **above ₹50 lakh up to ₹2 crore**, and the National Commission **above ₹2 crore** (limits can be revised). If a case is dismissed at the district level, the consumer can **appeal** to the State and then the National Commission.

Consumers can file complaints themselves, without a lawyer, and online through the **e-Daakhil** portal. Consumer groups (voluntary organisations called consumer forums or consumer protection councils) guide consumers and represent them.

steps.title: Standardisation and the way forward
steps.body:
- **ISI** (Indian Standards Institution mark, now certified by the **Bureau of Indian Standards, BIS**) – for industrial and consumer goods.
- **Agmark** – for agricultural products (honey, pulses, spices, ghee).
- **Hallmark** – for gold and silver jewellery (BIS).
- Certification is mandatory for products affecting health and safety (e.g. LPG cylinders, food colours and additives, cement, packaged drinking water).

The consumer movement still faces challenges: redressal can be slow and costly in time; many consumers are unaware; rules are not always enforced; adulteration persists. It needs consumers' voluntary effort and active participation.

steps.title: Solved example: Where should these complaints go? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Defective phone worth ₹30,000:** District Commission (up to ₹50 lakh).

**Step 2 – Faulty machinery worth ₹1.5 crore:** State Commission (above ₹50 lakh to ₹2 crore).

**Step 3 – Housing project worth ₹5 crore:** National Commission (above ₹2 crore).

steps.title: Solved example: Steps to file a consumer complaint (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Keep the bill, warranty card and evidence; first write to the seller/company.

**Step 2:** If unresolved, file a complaint at the appropriate commission (or online via e-Daakhil) with details and relief sought.

**Step 3:** Attend hearings; appeal to a higher commission if dissatisfied.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using old COPRA 1986 limits (₹20 lakh/₹1 crore) as current – rules under the 2019 Act revised them.
- Thinking a lawyer is compulsory – consumers can represent themselves.
- Mixing Agmark (farm products) with Hallmark (jewellery).

quiz.why: The consumer redressal system has three tiers: District, State and National Commissions.

He checks the invoice, writes to the platform and is ready to use the e-Daakhil portal.

steps.title: An alert consumer's checklist
steps.body:
- Read labels: MRP, net quantity, date of manufacture/expiry, ingredients, manufacturer address.
- Look for **ISI/BIS, Agmark, Hallmark** where applicable.
- Insist on a **bill**; keep warranty cards.
- Don't be swayed only by ads; compare.
- Complain first to the seller; then to consumer helplines or a commission. The **National Consumer Helpline** is **1915** (also 1800-11-4000).
- Join or support consumer awareness groups.

steps.title: Solved example: Case: A shop sells a ₹40 MRP soap for ₹45 (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Violation:** overcharging above MRP – right to be informed/unfair trade practice.

**Step 2 – Action:** refuse, ask for bill, complain to the helpline/legal metrology department or commission.

steps.title: Solved example: Case: A gold chain sold as 22-carat is found impure (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Check:** was it hallmarked? Hallmark assures purity.

**Step 2 – Redressal:** with the bill, file a complaint at the District Commission for refund/compensation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Throwing away the bill – it is key evidence.
- Waiting too long – complaints should generally be filed within **two years** of the cause of action.

questions.why: World Consumer Rights Day is observed on 15 March.

questions.why: Selling an expired snack violates the right to safety and the right to be informed.

questions.why: ISI or BIS marks show that electrical goods meet standards. Hallmark is for jewellery and Agmark for farm goods.

questions.why: A duty of consumers is to ask for a bill, because it is proof for complaints.

questions.q: Why is the consumer movement still weak in places?
options: Low awareness, slow redressal, poor enforcement
questions.why: The consumer movement is weak in places because of low awareness, slow redressal and poor enforcement.

questions.q: A complaint concerns goods worth ₹1.2 crore. Under the 2021 rules it goes to the
questions.why: Goods worth ₹50 lakh to ₹2 crore fall under the State Commission, so ₹1.2 crore goes there.

questions.q: A shopkeeper sells 950 g as 1 kg on 200 packets a day. How much sugar is the consumer cheated of daily?
questions.why: The shop gives 50 g less per packet. 50 g × 200 = 10,000 g, which is 10 kg a day.

questions.q: A product MRP is ₹80 but sold at ₹92. By what percentage is it overcharged?
questions.why: Overcharge = 92 − 80 = ₹12. As a share of MRP, 12 ÷ 80 = 15%.

options: food shortages, hoarding, black marketing and adulteration
questions.why: The movement arose because of food shortages, hoarding, black marketing and adulteration in the 1960s.

steps.title: Solved example: Write a 5-mark answer plan: “Salt March as an effective tool of resistance”
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Salt used by all – universal grievance.

**Step 2:** Letter of 11 demands (31 Jan 1930) ignored by Irwin.

**Step 3:** March from Sabarmati to Dandi (240 miles, 24 days), law broken 6 April.

**Step 4:** Mass civil disobedience – breaking salt and forest laws, boycotts.

steps.title: Solved example: Write a 3-mark answer plan: “Role of Bismarck”

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Losing marks for wrong dates – learn 10–15 anchor dates well.
- Writing long stories without points – examiners look for **key words**.

scenes.text: Rohan practises a blank map of India – dams, ports, airports, mines.
Map questions are easy marks if he knows the list.

steps.title: Key facts
steps.body:
- Soils: alluvial (most widespread), black/regur (cotton, Deccan trap), red/yellow (iron diffusion), laterite (leaching), arid, forest.
- Forest policy target 33% (1952). Wildlife Act 1972; Project Tiger 1973; JFM Odisha 1988.
- Dams: Bhakra Nangal (Sutlej–Beas), Hirakud (Mahanadi), Sardar Sarovar (Narmada), Tehri (Bhagirathi).
- Crops: rice >100 cm rain, >25°C; wheat 50–75 cm; cotton 210 frost-free days; rubber >200 cm; tea humus-rich soil.
- Minerals: magnetite up to 70% Fe, haematite 50–60%; Bailadila, Kudremukh; Khetri copper; Koraput bauxite; Koderma mica; lignite at Neyveli; Gondwana coal Damodar valley; Mumbai High oil.
- Industries: first cotton mill Mumbai 1854; first cement plant Chennai 1904; iron ore:coal:limestone ≈ 4:2:1; Bengaluru electronic capital.
- Transport: GQ Delhi–Kolkata–Chennai–Mumbai; N–S Srinagar–Kanyakumari; E–W Silchar–Porbandar; first train 1853 Bombay–Thane; NW-1 Ganga Prayagraj–Haldia.

steps.title: Map items to practise (CBSE-style list; check your year's list)
steps.body:
- **History:** Congress sessions – Calcutta (Sept 1920), Nagpur (Dec 1920), Madras (1927), Lahore (1929); movements – Champaran, Kheda, Ahmedabad, Amritsar (Jallianwala Bagh), Chauri Chaura, Dandi.
- **Geography:** major soil types; dams (Salal, Bhakra Nangal, Tehri, Rana Pratap Sagar, Sardar Sarovar, Hirakud, Nagarjuna Sagar, Tungabhadra); major crop areas (rice, wheat); iron ore mines, coal mines, oil fields; nuclear and thermal power plants; software technology parks; major sea ports (Kandla, Mumbai, Marmagao, New Mangalore, Kochi, Tuticorin, Chennai, Visakhapatnam, Paradip, Haldia, Kolkata); international airports.

**Step 1:** Higher sucrose content of cane.

**Step 2:** Cooler climate → longer crushing season.

- Placing Marmagao on the east coast – it is in **Goa** (west).

scenes.text: Arnav writes every Political Science concept as a one-line definition.
He then tests himself by covering the definitions.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Power sharing forms:** horizontal (organs), vertical (levels), social groups, parties/pressure groups.
- **Prudential vs moral** reasons.
- **Federalism:** two or more levels; constitutionally guaranteed jurisdictions; courts as umpire; coming together (USA) vs holding together (India).
- **Lists:** Union (defence, banking, currency), State (police, agriculture), Concurrent (education, forest, marriage); residuary → Union.
- **1992 amendments:** regular elections, reservations, one-third for women, State Election Commission, sharing powers/revenue.
- **Communalism** forms; **secular state** features.
- **Party recognition:** state – 6% votes + 2 assembly seats; national – 6% votes in LS or assemblies of 4 states + 4 LS seats.
- **Outcomes of democracy:** accountable, responsive, legitimate; growth; inequality; diversity; dignity.

steps.title: Solved example: Assertion–reason technique
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Judge A true/false on its own.

**Step 2:** Judge R true/false on its own.

**Step 3:** If both true, ask “Does R explain WHY A is true?” – use “because”. Example: A – Belgium avoided civil war; R – it shared power among communities → R explains A.

steps.title: Solved example: Case-based technique
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Underline the key situation words (e.g. “one language only”, “equal ministers”).

**Step 2:** Map them to a concept (majoritarianism / accommodation).

**Step 3:** Choose the option that names the concept and its effect.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling Hindi the national language.
- Saying panchayat elections are held by the Election Commission of India – it is the **State Election Commission**.

scenes.text: Economics numericals are quick marks: per capita income, IMR, BMI, interest.
Tara practises each once with units.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
- **Per capita income** = total income ÷ population.
- **IMR** = (infant deaths before age 1 ÷ live births) × 1,000.
- **BMI** = weight (kg) ÷ height² (m²); below 18.5 undernourished.
- **Literacy rate** – literate population aged 7+ as % of that age group.
- **Net attendance ratio** – children aged 14–15 attending school ÷ all children aged 14–15 × 100.
- **GDP** = value of final goods and services in a year (avoid double counting).
- **Simple interest** = P × R × T ÷ 100; monthly rate × 12 = annual simple rate.
- **Balance of trade** = exports − imports (positive = favourable).

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- Disguised unemployment; MGNREGA 2005 (100 days); organised/unorganised; public/private.
- Double coincidence of wants; demand deposits; collateral; terms of credit; formal/informal credit; SHGs (15–20 members).
- MNC; foreign investment; liberalisation (1991); trade barrier; WTO; SEZ; fair globalisation.
- Consumer rights: safety, information, choice, redressal, representation, education; three-tier commissions; ISI, Agmark, Hallmark.

steps.title: Solved example: Per capita income with unequal distribution
steps.body:
**Data:** incomes ₹3,000, ₹3,000, ₹4,000, ₹5,000, ₹35,000.

**Step 1:** Total = ₹50,000; average = ₹10,000.

**Step 2:** Four of five people earn below average → average hides inequality.

steps.title: Solved example: Compare two loans
steps.body:
**Data:** ₹25,000 for 1 year – bank 11% p.a.; moneylender 3% per month.

**Step 1:** Bank interest = ₹2,750.

**Step 2:** Moneylender = 36% p.a. → ₹9,000.

**Step 3:** Extra cost = ₹6,250.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting “× 1,000” in IMR.
- Adding intermediate goods to GDP.
- Treating monthly interest as annual.
